extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, students of poetry, and educated readers interested in poetic theory
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging poetic diction, meter, and the proper language of poetry versus prose; guidance on what makes verse genuinely poetic, natural, or prosaic. Emphasizes imagination, taste, and technical skill alongside avoidance of affectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of prosaic diction
rubrics_metrics.description: A poem may be blamable as 'prosaic' when 'the words and the order of the words would find their appropriate place in prose, but are not suitable to metrical composition.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test: if successive lines can be transcribed as prose without betraying that they were intended as verse (or by trivial word changes), they are prosaic. Examples given: parts of Daniel's CIVIL WARS are judged 'prosaic' because diction does not correspond to metre. Contrast with Spenser and Chaucer, where neutral diction still sits naturally in verse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sense and feeling as first condition
rubrics_metrics.description: Verses are not bad merely because they are 'unpoetic'; they are bad when they are empty of sense and feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even plain-language lines (colloquial phrasing) can be good if they have weight of sense and feeling and are treated with feeling; nursery-rhyme examples are not condemned for being 'unpoetic' but for emptiness of content. The subject must be interesting and treated with genuine feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meter must be audible, not merely visual
rubrics_metrics.description: Metre is the sole acknowledged formal difference between prose and verse; it should not be only 'metre to the eye' such that transcription into prose leaves lines unrecognizable as verse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a poem's metrical character disappears when read as prose (or after trivial restorations), the metre has been reduced to a visual artefact and the piece risks being prosaic. Blank verse is especially vulnerable because it can often be read as prose without alteration; rhymed verse may hide the problem by forced final words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of diction to metrical composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Words and their order must be suitable to metrical composition; diction appropriate in prose may still be unsuitable in metre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when language is correct, dignified, and the subject treated with feeling, the style can be prosaic if its lexis/order simply fits prose. The critic cites many examples (Daniel, some hymn-book and blank-verse passages) where otherwise good sense/feeling is marred by prosaic diction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grammar, logic, and psychology as governing principles
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should regulate style by 'the principles of grammar, logic, [and] psychology' and by a sound knowledge of material and spiritual facts—i.e., by good sense and taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the internal principles which distinguish a real poet from an impostor. Taste (the application of disciplined knowledge made instinctive) governs appropriate diction and avoids mere caprice. The resistance to arbitrary external rules is emphasized: the poet's craft rests on such principles rather than on slavish imitation of speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic language should arise from imagination/meditation, not mere imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should obtain language 'by the power of imagination proceeding upon the all in each of human nature' and by meditation rather than wandering to copy colloquial speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To distinguish subtle states (suppressed vs indulged anger, or rage vs jealousy) the poet must generalize from inward experience and imagination rather than simply copying rustic or market talk. Coleridge argues against Wordsworth's supposed prescription to copy the language of men in low life as an external rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish genuine poetic offspring from fashion/vanity
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic genius should 'distinguish by parental instinct its proper offspring from the changelings, which the gnomes of vanity or the fairies of fashion may have laid in its cradle.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules imposed from without will destroy poetry. The rules of the Imagination are formative powers; the outward words are mere outlines. A counterfeit (artifice) can mimic superficial form but lacks the internal vitality—'the marble peach feels cold and heavy.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid rhetorical caprices and forced juxtapositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures that excite by forced surprise or the apparent reconciliation of incompatible things (e.g., 'the hills are made to reflect the image of a voice') are rhetorical caprices—works of wit rather than of imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such compelled juxtapositions are not native to imagination and often indicate a voluntary, self-possessed cleverness incompatible with the steady fervour of a mind truly possessed by its subject. They are to be excluded from the honours of unaffected poetic fervour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neutral style (common to prose and verse) can be a legitimate excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: There exists a 'neutral style'—language common to prose and verse—which, when achieved, is a notable excellence: 'to seek only the apt expression of the thought, and yet to find at the same time with it the rhyme and the metre.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Garve's/Gellert's praise: poetry that reads like natural speech yet is perfectly fitted to metre and rhyme makes a great impression. Examples cited: Spenser, Chaucer, George Herbert, Waller, and others whose diction is natural yet dignified and metrically correct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical talent to find apt expression fitting rhyme and metre
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'talent...to seek only the apt expression of the thought, and yet to find at the same time with it the rhyme and the metre' is a rare and necessary skill for excellent verse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This technical facility — to express thought naturally while keeping syllabic measure and rhyme — is praised as producing poems that make a 'far greater impression than prose.' The poet must combine natural diction with metrical accuracy without sacrificing either.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject slavish reliance on colloquial speech as a universal rule
rubrics_metrics.description: It is insufficient and dangerous to limit poetic diction to the actual language of common life (market, wake, plough-field) as an absolute rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge concedes Wordsworth's preference for natural language in some subjects but argues against interpreting this as an exclusive prescription. The poet must use imagination and cultivated knowledge to elevate language beyond mere transcription of rustic speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid gaudy affectations and showy splendour
rubrics_metrics.description: A legitimate object of criticism is the 'gaudy affectations of a style' that pass for poetic diction but lack sense and common sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While Wordsworth sought to explode such splendour, Coleridge warns against over-correcting into a doctrine that excludes genuine poetic variety. Good criticism aims to establish principles of writing, not merely to condemn fashion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate authentic fervour from hysteric pseudo-poesy
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclude from poetic honours both 'the madness prepense of pseudopoesy' and the 'startling hysteric of weakness over-exerting itself'—i.e., artificial excitement posing as passion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: sensational odes to abstract terms (e.g., Odes to Jealousy, Hope) are often pseudo-poesy. True passionate expression arises from inward possession, not from forced rhetorical extravagance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and value individualized poetic voice
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet's diction may be so characteristic that short quotations are instantly recognizable as that poet's work; individuality of style is a legitimate and valuable quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge notes Wordsworth's highly individualized voice (e.g., 'The Child is father of the Man') and argues that uniform adherence to any single homely diction would suppress such characteristic individuality. Characteristic diction often increases poetic value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic rules must grow from imagination rather than be externally prescribed
rubrics_metrics.description: If a rule could be given from without that fully prescribed poetic diction, 'poetry would cease to be poetry, and sink into a mechanical art.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'rules of the Imagination' are internal powers of production and growth; external formulae reduce poetry to morphosis rather than poiaesis. Critics should therefore aim for principles, not rigid prescriptive formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate language to degree and kind of excitement
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet must know 'what differences of style it at once inspires and justifies; what intermixture of conscious volition is natural to that state' — i.e., match diction to subtlety of emotion (suppressed vs indulged anger, rage vs jealousy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This discrimination comes from imaginative insight and meditative generalization (the 'all in each'), not from naive observation. The poet's internal sense guides when a figure is natural or degenerates into ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware prosaisms detracting from merit
rubrics_metrics.description: The existence of prosaisms (prosaic lines) detracts from a poem's merit when they occur as frequent incorrespondency of diction to metre across compositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A writer may be valuable on other accounts yet legitimately be criticized as 'prosaic' if diction fails to fit metrical demands (the 'prosaic Daniel'). Conversely, many poets (Chaucer, Herbert, Spenser) exemplify neutral diction properly managed for verse.
